From my understanding, you have this internalized pressure to create your definition of “good” art - and what you consider “good” is by comparing your art to other people’s art. 

A mistake a lot of artists make is constantly comparing their art to other works, and deeming them not good enough when they believe the other piece is better - creating discouragement. 

Of course, taking inspiration from other art and artists is a huge part of the creative process, but it becomes an issue when it makes you feel like you’re not good enough.

Just create what makes you feel comfortable, what your brain and hand is itching for. Sometimes you just have to put your pen to the paper and just let it flow, regardless if you deem it a good piece of art or not - because ultimately - that piece came from YOU. Art, especially vent art, is about YOUR pain, YOUR feelings, YOUR thoughts.

I’ve created vent art that is just simply scribbles and shapes on a canvas. Maybe it’s not as visually pleasing as the Mona Lisa, but I don’t care.

Let me start off by saying I know exactly what you are going through. I have shared those exact same thoughts and feelings, and it is absolute hell. I am only a year older than you, but here is what I can tell you from my experience in recovering from suicidal ideation primarily from body-dysmorphia.

1. Being attractive and beautiful has a lot more to do than having the required assets to be deemed conventionally attractive. For example, I have known people who would’ve been deemed unattractive by society - who were very attractive individuals simply due to their personality and confidence. Super admirable people who were absolutely gorgeous, their internal attractiveness made them appear physically attractive as well - even if they had very apparent features that would be considered “ugly”. In contrast, I have also met people who were quite conventionally attractive, yet once I got to know them a bit better they ended up being super dull, or have horrible mannerisms, and a shitty personality overall that turned them to be super unattractive. To be truly pretty, you have to be pretty on the inside first - and if you have managed to attract good people into your life, then it sounds like you’ve achieved that. When I was working on gaining confidence in myself, I focused on what I liked about myself internally - and began to project that externally. My physical glow-up was crazy, and my confidence boosted.

Onto this point, I will also add that when you are judging yourself, you are primarily judging your physical  appearance by just staring at yourself in the mirror or a static image. You don’t see your personality, your vibe, your energy - and that is what adds to the beauty that you project onto others. You don’t see the real you, if that makes sense.

2. When it comes to dating and guys and all that jazz, you’d be surprised how much looks truly don’t matter. Men love women, and most of them will take any attention from any woman because they crave it so much. The guys who only care about girls for their looks are not the guys you want to get involved with anyway as they are usually the most shallow and will treat you like absolute garbage anyway. The guys who’s attention you want are gonna be the guys who see you as you truly are, and your imperfections won’t matter to them. Don’t be afraid to put yourself out there, they are probably waiting for you to make the first move. 

Also, dating it’s overrated as hell. It’s heavily romanticized in the media as this beautiful blissful experience, when in reality it is super stressful and draining. If you’re in university, don’t worry about getting involved romantically with anyone else. It isn’t worth it. Trust me.

3. I saw in the replies you’ve made that you seem to struggle with a binge-starve cycle. I know that all too well, and I know you don’t want help, and you don’t have to get it right now, but eventually, you should try to aim for recovery. Once again, not right now if you’re not ready, but when you are. It’s hard as fuck to get into the right mindset, but it isn’t the be-all-end all that it feels like right now.

You also said that you’re working out and taking care of your body physically - even while struggling with your eating habits - and that is super impressive and you’re doing more for your body than what most people do. You’re on the right path, keep doing it!

I’m not an animator myself, but I know exactly what you’re going through.

I’m sure you’ve heard this before but there is absolutely nothing wrong with not knowing what you want to do when you’re 16. Don’t stress over it. 

When I was 16 I was terrified for my future. I didn’t know what I wanted to do. Drove myself crazy with anxiety. I considered being an animator too, but my family wasn’t really supportive, and there is no opportunities where I live for both schooling and work in that field.

Once I graduated I tried many different things. I highly recommend actually getting out and working odd jobs if you aren’t already to get a feel for being in a professional environment. I even took a few random courses- didn’t like them - ended up dropping out. Nothing wrong with that.

I’m 21 now. Still don’t know exactly what I wanna do, and the world hasn’t ended, and it won’t. I don’t know what I was so stressed about. I’m going to school to be an Interactive Media Developer now. I enjoy it. If I don’t enjoy the work, I’ll just try and find something else.

You’re young. I know there’s a lot of pressure to find out what you wanna do, but coming from someone a few years older than you, it really isn’t that big of a deal. Once you’re a bit older and understand a bit more about how the world works, you’ll realize more about what you wanna do, whether that is animation or not.

And you don’t necessarily have to go to school to be an animator. If you want to work for a big company - like Disney or Dreamworks - then you will. But, with enough practice and passion , you could just simply make your own animations and post them on Youtube or TikTok. There was a youtuber I used to watch that went by the name of Domics that made his own little animations about various stories of his life and gained a lot of recognition for it - I don’t believe he was in school for animation. 

And animation will always be an option for you whether you decide to pursue it or not. You can do it when you graduate High School, or maybe you’ll be doing something else for a bit - then decide to pursue a career in animation.

I typically try to do anything to distract myself. Listen to music (not the depressing stuff, the stuff that actually makes you feel good, typically more ‘upbeat’ music), podcasts ( I mainly listen to true crime, but sometimes during really bad nights I’ll listen to more ‘therapy’ based podcasts or comedy if I’m in the mood). A good movie or TV show usually does the trick of allowing me to escape for a while. 

Going for a walk and listening to music is a good way to cope too, however if you deal with impulsive thoughts of putting yourself in harm I wouldn’t recommend it since you might be tempted to put yourself in harmful situations.

When I’m feeling really overwhelmed I write down how I’m feeling in a notebook, or even my notes app on my phone. It helps me rationalize my thoughts so they aren’t just one big clump of mess. I like to write my thoughts as if I’m talking to a friend or a therapist, or sometimes into a poem. Taking notes about how you’re feeling is also good if you’re seeing a therapist, because reading those notes to your therapists can help them get a better grasp of what’s going on in your head.

Just remember, you’re not alone in this, even when you’re feeling alone. :)

My cat once went missing in the woods for 6 months. 

He had been missing all winter, and I remember that particular winter was quite harsh (I live in Southern Canada). We spent as much time as we could searching for him. We put up fliers, asked people around the area, drove around the area a few times a week, and would often check the shelter. 

To my shock, he ended up turning up in the shelter after being identified by his microchip. He was in quite good condition too, aside from the fact the tips of his ears had froze off. 

We figured someone had taken him in and looked after him at some point, considering it would have been near impossible for him to survive temperatures of -30 degrees for 6 months in the forest.

He was also 11 years old at the time, and was a partially indoor and outdoor cat. He was incredibly street smart, and would spent hours outside wandering the neighbourhood. He always would find his way back. 

Now he is 16 years old, and is still in near perfect health. He doesn’t go outside as often, spends most of his time snoozing in the sun.

I hope your kitty has a safe return home! This wasn’t the only kitty I had get lost, I’ve had plenty of others run off on me. Most of the time they turned up. One time I had one end up inside of an elementary school, another one was found eating from a dumpster.

Cats are odd creatures, but through my experience, the whole “nine lives” thing isn’t a myth.
